metadata.title: Signal Representations on Graphs: Tools and Applications

nodes.name: Directed, irregular and weighted graph and degree vector
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G} = (\V,\E, \W)$ be a directed, irregular and weighted graph, where $\V = \{v_i \}_{i=1}^N$ is the set of nodes, $\E$ is the set of weighted edges, and $\W \in \R^{N \times N}$ is the weighted adjacency matrix, whose element $\W_{i,j}$ measures the underlying relation between the $i$th and the $j$th nodes. Let $\d \in \R^N$ be a degree vector, where $d_i = \sum_j \W_{i,j}$.
differentia: $\V = \{v_i \}_{i=1}^N$ is the set of nodes
$\E$ is the set of weighted edges
$\W \in \R^{N \times N}$ is the weighted adjacency matrix, whose element $\W_{i,j}$ measures the underlying relation between the $i$th and the $j$th nodes

nodes.name: Graph signal
nodes.statement: Given a fixed ordering of nodes, we assign a signal coefficient to each node; a~\emph{graph signal} is then defined as a vector, $$ \x = [x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_N]^T \in \R^N, $$ with $x_n$ the signal coefficient corresponding to the node $v_n$.
differentia: $\x = [x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_N]^T \in \R^N$
with $x_n$ the signal coefficient corresponding to the node $v_n$

nodes.name: Graph shift operator
nodes.statement: We use the graph shift operator $\Adj \in \R^{N \times N}$ as a graph representation, which is an elementary filtering operation that replaces a signal coefficient at a node with a weighted linear combination of coefficients at its neighboring nodes. Some common choices of a graph shift are weighted adjacency matrix $\W$, normalized adjacency matrix $\W_{\rm norm} = {\rm diag}(\d)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \W {\rm diag}(\d)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, and transition matrix $\Pj = {\rm diag}(\d)^{-1} \W$~\cite{ChenSMK:13}.
nodes.statement_short: The graph shift is a matrix graph representation performing one round of weighted neighbor averaging; common choices are $\W$, $\W_{\rm norm}$ and $\Pj$.
differentia: an elementary filtering operation that replaces a signal coefficient at a node with a weighted linear combination of coefficients at its neighboring nodes
nodes.origin_citation: algebraic signal processing, Pueschel & Moura 2008; Chen et al. 2013

nodes.name: Graph Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: The second one is based on the spectral graph theory~\cite{Chung:96}, where the graph Laplacian matrix $\LL \in \R^{N \times N}$ is used as a graph representation, which is a second-order difference operator on graphs. Some common choices of a graph Laplacian matrix are the unnormalized Laplacian ${\rm diag}(\d) - \W$, the normalized Laplacian $\Id - {\rm diag}(\d)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \W {\rm diag}(\d)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, and the transition Laplacian $\Id - {\rm diag}(\d)^{-1} \W $.
nodes.statement_short: The graph Laplacian is a second-order difference operator used as a graph representation, in unnormalized, normalized and transition forms.
differentia: a second-order difference operator on graphs

nodes.name: Graph structure matrix
nodes.statement: We use $\RR \in \R^{N \times N}$ to represent a graph structure matrix, which can be either a graph shift or a graph Laplacian matrix.
differentia: can be either a graph shift or a graph Laplacian matrix

nodes.name: Graph Fourier basis
nodes.statement: The~\textit{graph Fourier basis} $\Vm \in \R^{N \times N}$ is defined to be the eigenvector matrix of $\RR$, that is, \begin{equation*} \RR = \Vm \Lambda \Vm^{-1}, \end{equation*} where the $i$th column vector of $\Vm$ is the~\textit{graph Fourier basis vector} $\vv_i$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ as the $i$th diagonal element in $\Lambda$.
differentia: $\RR = \Vm \Lambda \Vm^{-1}$
the $i$th column vector of $\Vm$ is the~\textit{graph Fourier basis vector} $\vv_i$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$

nodes.name: Graph Fourier transform and inverse graph Fourier transform
nodes.statement: The graph Fourier transform \rm{of $\x \in \mathbb{R}^N$} is $ \widehat{\x} = \Um \x, $ where $\Um = \Vm^{-1}$ is called the graph Fourier transform matrix. When $\RR$ is symmetric, then $\Um = \Vm^T$ is orthornormal; the graph Fourier basis vector $\vv_i$ is the $i$th row vector of $\Um$. The~\textit{inverse graph Fourier transform} is $ \x = \Vm \widehat{\x}. $
nodes.statement_short: The graph Fourier transform is $\widehat{\x} = \Um\x$ with $\Um = \Vm^{-1}$; its inverse is $\x = \Vm\widehat{\x}$.
nodes.genus: linear transform of a graph signal
differentia: $ \widehat{\x} = \Um \x, $ where $\Um = \Vm^{-1}$ is called the graph Fourier transform matrix

nodes.name: Variation of a graph signal with respect to the graph shift
nodes.statement: When the graph representation matrix is the graph shift, the variation of a graph signal $\x$ is defined as, \begin{equation*} \STV_{\Adj} ( \x ) = \left\| \x - \frac{1}{\left\lvert\lambda_{\max}(\Adj)\right\rvert} \Adj \x \right\|_2^2, \end{equation*} where $\lambda_{\max}(\Adj)$ is the eigenvalue of $\Adj$ with the largest magnitude.
differentia: $\STV_{\Adj} ( \x ) = \left\| \x - \frac{1}{\left\lvert\lambda_{\max}(\Adj)\right\rvert} \Adj \x \right\|_2^2$

nodes.name: Variation of a graph signal with respect to the graph Laplacian
nodes.statement: When the graph representation matrix is the graph Laplacian matrix, the variation of a graph signal $\x$ is defined as, \begin{equation*} \STV_{\LL} (\x) = \sum_{i,j=1}^N \Adj_{i,j}(x_i-x_j)^2 = \x^T \LL \x. \end{equation*}
differentia: $\STV_{\LL} (\x) = \sum_{i,j=1}^N \Adj_{i,j}(x_i-x_j)^2 = \x^T \LL \x$

nodes.name: Ordering of graph shift eigenvector variations
nodes.statement: We can show that when the eigenvalues of the graph shift $\Adj $ are sorted in a nonincreasing order $\lambda^{(\Adj)}_1 \geq \lambda^{(\Adj)}_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda^{(\Adj)}_N$, the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follow a nondecreasing order $\STV_{\Adj}(\vv^{(\Adj)}_1) \leq \STV_{(\Adj)}(\vv^{(\Adj)}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \STV_{(\Adj)}(\vv^{(\Adj)}_N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sorting graph-shift eigenvalues in nonincreasing order sorts the eigenvector variations in nondecreasing order.
assumptions: the eigenvalues of the graph shift $\Adj $ are sorted in a nonincreasing order $\lambda^{(\Adj)}_1 \geq \lambda^{(\Adj)}_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda^{(\Adj)}_N$
conclusions: the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follow a nondecreasing order $\STV_{\Adj}(\vv^{(\Adj)}_1) \leq \STV_{(\Adj)}(\vv^{(\Adj)}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \STV_{(\Adj)}(\vv^{(\Adj)}_N)$

nodes.name: Ordering of graph Laplacian eigenvector variations
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can show that when the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian $\LL$ are sorted in a nondecreasing order $\lambda^{(\LL)}_1 \leq \lambda^{(\LL)}_2 \leq \ldots \leq \lambda^{(\LL)}_N$, the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follows a nondecreasing order $\STV_{\LL}(\vv^{(\LL)}_1) \leq \STV_{\LL}(\vv^{(\LL)}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \STV_{\LL}(\vv^{(\LL)}_N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sorting Laplacian eigenvalues in nondecreasing order sorts the eigenvector variations in nondecreasing order.
assumptions: the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian $\LL$ are sorted in a nondecreasing order $\lambda^{(\LL)}_1 \leq \lambda^{(\LL)}_2 \leq \ldots \leq \lambda^{(\LL)}_N$
conclusions: the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follows a nondecreasing order $\STV_{\LL}(\vv^{(\LL)}_1) \leq \STV_{\LL}(\vv^{(\LL)}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \STV_{\LL}(\vv^{(\LL)}_N)$

nodes.name: Low-frequency and high-frequency components
nodes.statement: The variations of graph Fourier basis vectors thus allow us to provide the ordering: the Fourier basis vectors with small variations are considered as \textit{low-frequency} components while the vectors with large variations are considered as \textit{high-frequency} components~\cite{SandryhailaM:131}.
differentia: with small variations are considered as \textit{low-frequency} components
with large variations are considered as \textit{high-frequency} components

nodes.name: Graph Fourier bases ordered low to high frequency
nodes.statement: In the following discussion, we assume all graph Fourier bases are ordered from low frequencies to high frequencies.

nodes.name: Representation-based framework with three components
nodes.statement: In this section, we introduce a representation-based framework with three components, including graph signal models, representation dictionaries and the related tasks, in a general and abstract level. This lays a foundation for the following sections, which are essentially special cases that follow this general framework.

nodes.name: Descriptive approach to a graph signal model
nodes.statement: For the descriptive approach, we describe the properties of a graph signal by bounding the output of some operator. Let $\x$ be a graph signal, $f(\cdot)$ be a function operating on $\x$, we define a class of graph signals by restricting \begin{equation} f(\x) \leq C, \end{equation} where $C$ is some constant. For example, we define smooth graph signals by restricting $\x^T \LL \x$ be small~\cite{BelkinNS:06}.
nodes.statement_short: The descriptive approach defines a signal class by bounding an operator output, $f(\x)\le C$.
nodes.genus: way to mathematically model a graph signal
differentia: we describe the properties of a graph signal by bounding the output of some operator
we define a class of graph signals by restricting $f(\x) \leq C$

nodes.name: Generative approach to a graph signal model
nodes.statement: For the generative approach, we describe the properties of a graph signal by using a graph dictionary. Let $\D$ be a graph dictionary, we define a class of graph signals by restricting \begin{equation*} \x \ = \ \D \a, \end{equation*} where $\a$ is a vector of expansion coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: The generative approach defines a signal class as everything a dictionary can synthesize, $\x = \D\a$.
nodes.genus: way to mathematically model a graph signal
differentia: we describe the properties of a graph signal by using a graph dictionary
we define a class of graph signals by restricting $\x \ = \ \D \a$

nodes.name: Passive approach to graph dictionary design
nodes.statement: For the passive approach, the graph dictionary is designed only based on the graph structure; that is, \begin{equation*} \D = g(\RR), \end{equation*} where $g(\cdot)$ is some operator on the graph structure matrix $\RR$.
nodes.genus: approach to design a graph dictionary
differentia: the graph dictionary is designed only based on the graph structure

nodes.name: Active approach to graph dictionary design
nodes.statement: For the active approach, the graph dictionary is designed based on both graph structure and a set of given graph signals; that is, \begin{equation*} \D = g(\Adj, \X), \end{equation*} where $\X$ is a matrix representation of a set of graph signals.
nodes.genus: approach to design a graph dictionary
differentia: the graph dictionary is designed based on both graph structure and a set of given graph signals
$\D = g(\Adj, \X)$

nodes.name: Frame bounds property of a graph dictionary
nodes.statement: Frame bounds. For any $\x$ in a certain graph signal model, \begin{equation*} \alpha_1 \left\| \x \right\|_2 \leq \left\| \D \x \right\|_2 \leq \alpha_2 \left\| \x \right\|_2, \end{equation*} where $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ are some constants;
nodes.genus: standard property of a graph dictionary $\D$
differentia: $\alpha_1 \left\| \x \right\|_2 \leq \left\| \D \x \right\|_2 \leq \alpha_2 \left\| \x \right\|_2$ for any $\x$ in a certain graph signal model

nodes.name: Sparse representations property of a graph dictionary
nodes.statement: Sparse representations. For any $\x$ in a certain graph signal model, there exists a sparse coefficient $\a$ with $\left\| \a \right\|_0 \leq C$, which satisfies \begin{equation*} \left\| \x - \D \a \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon, \end{equation*} where $C, \epsilon$ are some constants;
nodes.genus: standard property of a graph dictionary $\D$
differentia: there exists a sparse coefficient $\a$ with $\left\| \a \right\|_0 \leq C$, which satisfies $\left\| \x - \D \a \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon$

nodes.name: Uncertainty principles property of a graph dictionary
nodes.statement: Uncertainty principles. For any $\x$ in a certain graph signal model, the following is satisfied \begin{equation*} \left\| \a_1 \right\|_0 + \left\| \a_2 \right\|_0 \geq C, \end{equation*} where $\left\| \x - \D_1 \a_1 \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon$ and $\left\| \x - \D_2 \a_2 \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon$, and $\D = \begin{bmatrix} \D_1 & \D_2 \end{bmatrix}$.
nodes.genus: standard property of a graph dictionary $\D$
differentia: $\left\| \a_1 \right\|_0 + \left\| \a_2 \right\|_0 \geq C$
$\left\| \x - \D_1 \a_1 \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon$ and $\left\| \x - \D_2 \a_2 \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon$, and $\D = \begin{bmatrix} \D_1 & \D_2 \end{bmatrix}$

nodes.name: Sparse coding problem for approximation
nodes.statement: We consider approximating a graph signal by using a linear combination of a few atoms from $\D$ and solving the following sparse coding problem, \begin{eqnarray} \x^*, \a^*= & \arg \min_{\x, \a} & d(\x', \x ), \\ \nonumber & {\rm subject~to:~} & \x' = \D \a, \\ \nonumber && \left\| \a \right\|_0 \leq K. \end{eqnarray} where $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ is some evaluation metric.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $\x$ by at most $K$ dictionary atoms, minimizing an evaluation metric $d(\x',\x)$.

nodes.name: Sampling pattern matrix and sampling operator
nodes.statement: Let $\F \in \R^{N \times N}$ be a sampling pattern matrix, which is constrained by a given application and the sampling operator is \begin{equation} \Psi = \Cc \F \in \R^{M \times N}, \end{equation} where $\Cc \in \R^{M \times N}$ selects rows from $\F$.
differentia: $\Psi = \Cc \F \in \R^{M \times N}$
$\Cc \in \R^{M \times N}$ selects rows from $\F$

nodes.name: Uniform, experimentally designed and active sampling strategies
nodes.statement: There are three sampling strategies: (1) uniform sampling when designing $\Cc$, , where row indices are chosen from from $\{0, 1, \cdots, N-1\}$ independently and uniformly; and~\emph{experimentally design sampling}, where row indices can be chosen beforehand; and~\emph{active sampling}, where we will use feedback as samples are sequentially collected to decide the next row to be sampled. Each sampling strategy can be implemented by two approaches, including a random approach and a deterministic one. The sampling pattern matrix $\F$ constraints the following sampling patterns: when $\F$ is an identity matrix, $\Psi$ is a subsampling operator; when $\F$ is a Gaussian random matrix, $\Psi$ is a compressed sampling operator.
nodes.statement_short: Three sampling strategies (uniform, experimentally designed, active), each realizable randomly or deterministically; $\F$ fixes whether $\Psi$ subsamples or compresses.

nodes.name: Prototype of designing sampling and recovery strategies
nodes.statement: The prototype of designing sampling and recovery strategies is \begin{eqnarray*} \Psi^*(\D), \Phi^*(\D) = \min_{\Psi, \Phi} \max_{\a} && d(\x', \x), \\ {\rm subject~to} && \x' = \Phi \Psi (\x + \epsilon), \\ && \x = \D \a, \end{eqnarray*} where $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ is some evaluation metric.
nodes.statement_short: Minimax design of a sampling operator $\Psi$ and recovery operator $\Phi$ over signals generated by a dictionary $\D$.

nodes.name: Pairwise Lipschitz smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ with unit norm is~\emph{pairwise Lipschitz smooth} with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} | x_i - x_j | \ \leq \ C \ d(v_i, v_j),~{\rm for~all~} i,j = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1, \end{equation*} with $d(v_i, v_j)$ the distance between the $i$th and the $j$th nodes.
nodes.genus: a graph signal $\x$ with unit norm
differentia: $| x_i - x_j | \ \leq \ C \ d(v_i, v_j),~{\rm for~all~} i,j = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1$

nodes.name: Total Lipschitz smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ with unit norm is~\emph{total Lipschitz smooth} with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \sum_{(i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} ( x_i - x_j )^2 \ \leq \ C. \end{equation*}
nodes.genus: a graph signal $\x$ with unit norm
differentia: $\sum_{(i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} ( x_i - x_j )^2 \ \leq \ C$

nodes.name: Local normalized neighboring smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ with unit norm is~\emph{local normalized neighboring smooth } with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j: (i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} } \sum_{j: (i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \ \leq \ C. \end{equation*}
nodes.genus: a graph signal $\x$ with unit norm
differentia: $\sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j: (i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} } \sum_{j: (i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \ \leq \ C$

nodes.name: Global normalized neighboring smooth graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ with unit norm is~\emph{global normalized neighboring smooth} with parameter $C$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{ |\lambda_{\max}(\W)| } \sum_{j: (i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \ \leq \ C. \end{equation*}
nodes.genus: a graph signal $\x$ with unit norm
differentia: $\sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{ |\lambda_{\max}(\W)| } \sum_{j: (i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \ \leq \ C$

nodes.name: Polynomial graph signal and graph polynomial dictionary
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ is polynomial with degree $K$ when \begin{equation*} \x \ = \ \D_{\rm poly(K)} \a \ = \ \begin{bmatrix} {\bf 1} & \D^{(1)} & \D^{(2)} & \ldots & \D^{(K)} \end{bmatrix} \a \in \R^N, \end{equation*} where $\a \in \R^{KN+1}$ and $\D_{\rm poly(K)} $ is a graph polynomial dictionary with $\D^{(k)}_{i,j} = d^k(v_i, v_j)$. Denote this class by $\PL(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: A signal is polynomial of degree $K$ when it is a linear combination of atoms of powers of node distances, $\D^{(k)}_{i,j}=d^k(v_i,v_j)$.
nodes.definiendum: polynomial graph signal with degree $K$, class $\PL(K)$
differentia: $\x \ = \ \D_{\rm poly(K)} \a$
$\D_{\rm poly(K)} $ is a graph polynomial dictionary with $\D^{(k)}_{i,j} = d^k(v_i, v_j)$

nodes.name: Classical polynomial time signals versus graph polynomial signals
nodes.statement: In classical signal processing, polynomial time signals can be expressed as $x_n = \sum_{k=0}^K a_k n^k$, $n = 1, \ldots, N$; we can rewrite this as in the above definition as $\x = \D_{K} \a$, with $(D_K)_{n,k} = n^k$. The columns of $\D_{K}$ are denoted as $\D^{(k)}$, $k = 0, \ldots, K$, and called \emph{atoms}; the elements of each atom $\D^{(k)}$ are $n^k$. Since polynomial time signals are shift-invariant, we can set any time point as the origin; such signals are thus characterized by $K+1$ degrees of freedom $a_k$, $k = 0, \ldots, K$. This is not true for graph signals, however; they are not shift-invariant and any node can serve as the origin (see Figure~\ref{fig:origin}). In the above definition, $\D^{(k)}$ are now matrices with the number of atoms equal to the number of nodes $N$ (with each atom corresponding to the node serving as the origin). The dictionary $\D_{K}$ thus contains $KN+1$ atoms.
nodes.statement_short: Classical polynomial signals need $K+1$ coefficients, but graphs lack shift invariance so every node can be an origin, giving $KN+1$ atoms.

nodes.name: Graph polynomial dictionary represents the pairwise Lipschiz smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf Graph polynomial dictionary represents the pairwise Lipschiz smooth signals}) $\PL(1)$ is a subset of the pairwise Lipschitz smooth with some parameter $C$.
conclusions: $\PL(1)$ is a subset of the pairwise Lipschitz smooth with some parameter $C$

nodes.name: Proof that $\PL(1)$ is pairwise Lipschitz smooth
nodes.statement: Let $\x \in \PL(1)$, that is, $$ \x = \begin{bmatrix} {\bf 1} & \D^{(1)} \end{bmatrix} \a, $$ Then, we write the pairwise Lipschitz smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} |x_i - x_j| & = & | \sum_{k} \left( d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) \right) a_k | \\ & \leq & \sum_{k} | d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) | |a_k | \\ \\ & \leq & \sum_{k} |a_k | | d(v_i, v_j) | \ = \ \left\| \a \right\|_1 | d(v_i, v_j) |. \end{eqnarray*} The parameter $C = \left\| \a \right\|_1$, which corresponds to the energy of the original graph signal.
nodes.statement_short: Direct expansion plus the triangle inequality for the distance metric, giving $C = \|\a\|_1$.

nodes.name: Expand a degree-1 polynomial signal
nodes.statement: Let $\x \in \PL(1)$, that is, $$ \x = \begin{bmatrix} {\bf 1} & \D^{(1)} \end{bmatrix} \a, $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the degree-1 polynomial expansion of $\x$.

nodes.name: Bound the pairwise difference by the triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Then, we write the pairwise Lipschitz smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} |x_i - x_j| & = & | \sum_{k} \left( d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) \right) a_k | \\ & \leq & \sum_{k} | d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) | |a_k | \\ \\ & \leq & \sum_{k} |a_k | | d(v_i, v_j) | \ = \ \left\| \a \right\|_1 | d(v_i, v_j) |. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the triangle inequality twice to bound $|x_i-x_j|$ by $\|\a\|_1 d(v_i,v_j)$.

nodes.name: Identify the Lipschitz parameter
nodes.statement: The parameter $C = \left\| \a \right\|_1$, which corresponds to the energy of the original graph signal.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude that the Lipschitz constant is $\|\a\|_1$.

nodes.name: Bandlimited graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ is bandlimited with respect to a graph Fourier basis $\Vm$ with bandwidth $K$ when \begin{equation*} \x = \Vm_{(K)} \a, \end{equation*} where $\a \in \R^{K}$ and $\Vm_{(K)}$ is a submatrix containing the first $K$ columns of $\Vm$. Denote this class by $\BL_{\Vm}(K)$~\cite{ChenVSK:15}.
differentia: $\Vm_{(K)}$ is a submatrix containing the first $K$ columns of $\Vm$

nodes.name: Bandlimited classes match the three smoothness criteria
nodes.statement: When $\Vm$ is the eigenvector matrix of the unnormalized graph Laplacian matrix, we denote it as $\Vm_{\LL}$ and can show that signals in $\BL_{\Vm_{\LL}}(K)$ are total Lipschitz smooth; when $\Vm$ is the eigenvector matrix of the transition matrix, we denote it as $\Vm_{\Pj}$ and can show that signals in $\BL_{\Vm_{\Pj}}(K)$ are local normalized neighboring smooth; when $\Vm$ is the eigenvector matrix of the weighted adjacency matrix, we denote it as $\Vm_{\W}$ and can show that signals in $\BL_{\Vm_{\W}}(K)$ are global normalized neighboring smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Bandlimited signals of $\Vm_\LL$, $\Vm_\Pj$, $\Vm_\W$ satisfy respectively the total-Lipschitz, local- and global-normalized-neighboring smoothness criteria.
assumptions: $\Vm$ is the eigenvector matrix of the unnormalized graph Laplacian matrix
$\Vm$ is the eigenvector matrix of the transition matrix
$\Vm$ is the eigenvector matrix of the weighted adjacency matrix
conclusions: signals in $\BL_{\Vm_{\LL}}(K)$ are total Lipschitz smooth
signals in $\BL_{\Vm_{\Pj}}(K)$ are local normalized neighboring smooth
signals in $\BL_{\Vm_{\W}}(K)$ are global normalized neighboring smooth

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian represents the total Lipschiz smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian represents the total Lipschiz smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\BL_{\Vm_{\LL}}(K)$ is a subset of the total Lipschitz smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq \lambda^{(\LL)}_k$.
assumptions: For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$
when $C \geq \lambda^{(\LL)}_k$
conclusions: $\BL_{\Vm_{\LL}}(K)$ is a subset of the total Lipschitz smooth with parameter $C$

nodes.name: Proof that Laplacian-bandlimited signals are total Lipschitz smooth
nodes.statement: Let $\x$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is, $$ \x = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\LL)}_k, $$ Then, we write the total Lipschitz smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} && \sum_{(i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} ( x_i - x_j )^2 \ = \ \x^T \LL \x \\ & = & (\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\LL)}_k)^T (\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k \lambda_k \vv^{(\LL)}_k) \ = \ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda^{(\LL)}_k \widehat{x}_k^2 \\ & \leq & \lambda^{(\LL)}_K \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k^2 \ = \ \lambda^{(\LL)}_K. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\x^T\LL\x$ in the Laplacian eigenbasis and bound each eigenvalue by $\lambda^{(\LL)}_K$.

nodes.name: Write the bandlimited expansion
nodes.statement: Let $\x$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is, $$ \x = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\LL)}_k, $$
nodes.statement_short: Set up $\x$ as a combination of the first $K$ Laplacian eigenvectors.

nodes.name: Evaluate and bound the Laplacian quadratic form
nodes.statement: Then, we write the total Lipschitz smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} && \sum_{(i,j) \in \E} \W_{i,j} ( x_i - x_j )^2 \ = \ \x^T \LL \x \\ & = & (\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\LL)}_k)^T (\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k \lambda_k \vv^{(\LL)}_k) \ = \ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda^{(\LL)}_k \widehat{x}_k^2 \\ & \leq & \lambda^{(\LL)}_K \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k^2 \ = \ \lambda^{(\LL)}_K. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize the quadratic form and bound it by the largest retained eigenvalue.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the transition matrix represents the local normalized neighboring smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the transition matrix represents the local normalized neighboring smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\BL_{\Vm_{\Pj}}(K)$ is a subset of the local normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K})^2$.
assumptions: For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$
when $C \geq (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K})^2$
conclusions: $\BL_{\Vm_{\Pj}}(K)$ is a subset of the local normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$

nodes.name: Proof that transition-matrix-bandlimited signals are local normalized neighboring smooth
nodes.statement: Let $\x$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is, $$ \x = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\Pj)}_k, $$ Then, we write the local normalized neighboring smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} && \left| x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} } \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} x_j \right| \\ &= & \left| \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\Pj)}_k \right)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \Pj_{i,j} \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\Pj)}_k \right)_j \right| \\ & = & \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \left( (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \Pj_{i,j} (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_j \right) \right| \\ & = & \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k (1 - \lambda_k) (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_i \right| \\ & \leq & (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K}) \left| \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_i \right| \ = \ (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K}) |x_i|. \end{eqnarray*} The last equality follows from the fact that $\vv^{(\Pj)}_k$ and $\lambda^{(\Pj)}_k$ are eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $\Pj$. \begin{eqnarray*} && \sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i }} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i } \W_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} |x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} } \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} x_j |^2 \\ & \leq & \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K} )^2 |x_i|^2 \ = \ (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K})^2 . \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the per-node neighboring difference by $(1-\lambda^{(\Pj)}_K)|x_i|$ using the eigen-relation of $\Pj$, then sum over nodes.

nodes.name: Write the bandlimited expansion in the transition eigenbasis
nodes.statement: Let $\x$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is, $$ \x = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\Pj)}_k, $$
nodes.statement_short: Set up $\x$ as a combination of the first $K$ eigenvectors of $\Pj$.

nodes.name: Bound the per-node neighboring difference
nodes.statement: Then, we write the local normalized neighboring smooth criterion as \begin{eqnarray*} && \left| x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} } \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} x_j \right| \\ &= & \left| \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\Pj)}_k \right)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \Pj_{i,j} \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \vv^{(\Pj)}_k \right)_j \right| \\ & = & \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \left( (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \Pj_{i,j} (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_j \right) \right| \\ & = & \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k (1 - \lambda_k) (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_i \right| \\ & \leq & (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K}) \left| \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k (\vv^{(\Pj)}_k)_i \right| \ = \ (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K}) |x_i|. \end{eqnarray*} The last equality follows from the fact that $\vv^{(\Pj)}_k$ and $\lambda^{(\Pj)}_k$ are eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $\Pj$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the eigen-relation of $\Pj$ to bound each node's neighboring difference by $(1-\lambda^{(\Pj)}_K)|x_i|$.

nodes.name: Sum over all nodes to obtain the criterion constant
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray*} && \sum_i \left( x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i }} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i } \W_{i,j} x_j \right)^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} |x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} } \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \W_{i,j} x_j |^2 \\ & \leq & \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K} )^2 |x_i|^2 \ = \ (1 - \lambda^{(\Pj)}_{K})^2 . \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Sum the per-node bounds and use unit norm to conclude $C=(1-\lambda^{(\Pj)}_K)^2$.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the adjacency matrix represents the global normalized neighboring smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the adjacency matrix represents the global normalized neighboring smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\BL_{\Vm_{\W}}(K)$ is a subset of the global normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq (1 - \lambda^{(\W)}_{K} / |\lambda_{\max}{(\W)}| )^2$.
assumptions: For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$
when $C \geq (1 - \lambda^{(\W)}_{K} / |\lambda_{\max}{(\W)}| )^2$
conclusions: $\BL_{\Vm_{\W}}(K)$ is a subset of the global normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$

nodes.name: Proof similar to the transition-matrix theorem; eigenvalue ordering conventions
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to Theorem~\ref{thm:LNNS}. Note that for graph Laplacian, the eigenvalues are sorted in an ascending order; for the transition matrix and the adjacency matrix, the eigenvalues are sorted in a descending order.

nodes.name: Correspondence between the three models and the four smoothness criteria
nodes.statement: Each of these three models generates smooth graph signals according to one of the four criteria in Definitions~\ref{df:pairwise_Lip},~\ref{df:global_Lip},~\ref{df:local_neighboring_smooth} and~\ref{df:global_neighboring_smooth}: $\PL(K)$ models Lipschitz smooth signals; $\BL_{\Vm_{\LL}}(K)$ models total Lipschitz smooth signals; $\BL_{\Vm_{\Pj}}(K)$ with models the local normalized neighboring smooth signals; and $\BL_{\Vm_{\W}}(K)$ models the global normalized neighboring smooth signals; the corresponding graph representation dictionaries are $\D_{\rm poly(K)}$, $\Vm_{\LL}$, $\Vm_{\Pj}$, and $\Vm_{\W}$.
nodes.statement_short: Maps each generative model to the smoothness criterion it realizes and to its representation dictionary.

nodes.name: Frame bounds of the smooth graph dictionaries
nodes.statement: Graph polynomial dictionary is highly redundant and the frame bound is loose. When the graph is undirected, the adjacency matrix is symmetric, then $\Vm_{\LL}$ and $\Vm_{\W}$ are orthonormal.

nodes.name: Frame bounds for directed graphs
nodes.statement: It is hard to draw any meaningful conclusion when the graph is directed; we leave it for the future work.

nodes.name: Sparse representations of the smooth graph dictionaries
nodes.statement: Graph polynomial dictionary provides sparse representations for polynomial graph signals. On the other hand, the graph Fourier bases provide sparse representations for the bandlimited graph signals. For approximately bandlimited graph signals, there are some residuals coming from the high-frequency components.

nodes.name: $\epsilon$-vertex concentrated graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ is~\emph{$\epsilon$-vertex concentrated} on a graph vertex set $\Gamma$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \left\| \x - \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon, \end{equation*} where $\Id_{\Gamma} \in \R^{N \times N}$ is a diagonal matrix, with $(\Id_{\Gamma})_{i,i} = 1$ when $i \in \Gamma$ and $0$, otherwise.
differentia: $\left\| \x - \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon$ on a graph vertex set $\Gamma$

nodes.name: $\epsilon$-spectrum concentrated graph signal
nodes.statement: A graph signal $\x$ is~\emph{$\epsilon$-spectrum concentrated} on a graph spectrum band $\Omega$ when it satisfies \begin{equation*} \left\| \x - \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \x \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon, \end{equation*} where $ \Vm_{\Omega} \in \R^{N \times |\Omega|}$ is a submatrix of $\Vm$ with columns selected by $\Omega$ and $ \Um_{\Omega} \in \R^{|\Omega| \times N}$ is a submatrix of $\Vm$ with rows selected by $\Omega$.
differentia: $\left\| \x - \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \x \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon$ on a graph spectrum band $\Omega$

nodes.name: Uncertainty principle of the graph vertex and spectrum domains
nodes.statement: ({\bf Uncertainty principle of the graph vertex and spectrum domains}) Let a unit norm signal $\x$ supported on an undirected graph be $\epsilon_{\Gamma}$-vertex concentrated and $\epsilon_{\Omega}$-spectrum concentrated at the same time. Then, \begin{equation*} |\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega| \geq \frac{(1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ))^2 }{ \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 }. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: A signal concentrated both on $\Gamma$ vertices and on band $\Omega$ forces $|\Gamma||\Omega|$ to be large, with the bound scaled by $\|\Um_\Omega\|_\infty^{-2}$.
assumptions: Let a unit norm signal $\x$ supported on an undirected graph be $\epsilon_{\Gamma}$-vertex concentrated and $\epsilon_{\Omega}$-spectrum concentrated at the same time
conclusions: $|\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega| \geq \frac{(1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ))^2 }{ \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 }$

nodes.name: Proof of the graph uncertainty principle
nodes.statement: We first show $\left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_2 \leq \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty} \sqrt{ |\Gamma|\cdot |\Omega|}$. \begin{eqnarray*} && ( \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x )_s \ = \ \sum_{k \in \Omega} \Vm_{s,k} \left( \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \Um_{k,i} x_i \right) \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left( \sum_{k \in \Omega} \Vm_{s,k} \Um_{k,i} \right) x_i \ = \ \sum_i q(s,i) x_i, \end{eqnarray*} where \begin{equation*} q(s,i) = \left\{ \begin{array}{rl} \sum_{k \in \Omega} \Vm_{s,k} \Um_{k,i}, & i \in \Gamma;\\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}. \end{array} \right. \end{equation*} Let $\y^{(i)}$ be a graph signal with $y^{(i)}_s = q(s,i)$. Then, $( \widehat{\y^{(i)}} )_k = {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \Um_{k,i}$. We then have \begin{eqnarray*} && \left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_{2}^2 \ \leq \ \left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_{\rm HS}^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{s} |q(s,i)|^2 \ = \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \y^{(i)} \right\|_2^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \widehat{ \y^{(i)} } \right\|_2^2 \ = \ \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} \left( {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \Um_{k,i} \right)^2 \\ & \leq & \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \ = \ \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 |\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega|. \end{eqnarray*} We then show that $\left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 \geq 1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} )$. Based on the assumption, we have \begin{eqnarray*} && \left\| \x - \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 \\ & = & \left\| \x - \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 + \left\| \Id_{\Gamma} \x - \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 \\ & \leq & \epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma}. \end{eqnarray*} Since $\x$ has a unit norm, by the triangle inequality, we have \begin{equation*} \left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_2 \geq 1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ). \end{equation*} Finally, we combine two results and obtain \begin{equation*} |\Gamma|\cdot |\Omega| \geq \frac{\left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_2^2}{\left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 } \ > \ \frac{ (1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ))^2 }{ \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich the operator norm of $\Vm_\Omega\Um_\Omega\Id_\Gamma$: upper-bound it by Hilbert-Schmidt norm, lower-bound it by the triangle inequality, then combine.

nodes.name: Upper bound the operator norm via the Hilbert-Schmidt norm
nodes.statement: We first show $\left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_2 \leq \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty} \sqrt{ |\Gamma|\cdot |\Omega|}$. \begin{eqnarray*} && ( \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x )_s \ = \ \sum_{k \in \Omega} \Vm_{s,k} \left( \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \Um_{k,i} x_i \right) \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left( \sum_{k \in \Omega} \Vm_{s,k} \Um_{k,i} \right) x_i \ = \ \sum_i q(s,i) x_i, \end{eqnarray*} where \begin{equation*} q(s,i) = \left\{ \begin{array}{rl} \sum_{k \in \Omega} \Vm_{s,k} \Um_{k,i}, & i \in \Gamma;\\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}. \end{array} \right. \end{equation*} Let $\y^{(i)}$ be a graph signal with $y^{(i)}_s = q(s,i)$. Then, $( \widehat{\y^{(i)}} )_k = {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \Um_{k,i}$. We then have \begin{eqnarray*} && \left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_{2}^2 \ \leq \ \left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_{\rm HS}^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{s} |q(s,i)|^2 \ = \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \y^{(i)} \right\|_2^2 \\ & = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \widehat{ \y^{(i)} } \right\|_2^2 \ = \ \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} \left( {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \Um_{k,i} \right)^2 \\ & \leq & \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \ = \ \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 |\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega|. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the kernel $q(s,i)$ and bound the spectral norm by the Hilbert-Schmidt norm, giving $\|\Um_\Omega\|_\infty\sqrt{|\Gamma||\Omega|}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound the operator norm from the concentration assumptions
nodes.statement: We then show that $\left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 \geq 1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} )$. Based on the assumption, we have \begin{eqnarray*} && \left\| \x - \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 \\ & = & \left\| \x - \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 + \left\| \Id_{\Gamma} \x - \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \x \right\|_2 \\ & \leq & \epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma}. \end{eqnarray*} Since $\x$ has a unit norm, by the triangle inequality, we have \begin{equation*} \left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_2 \geq 1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Use vertex and spectrum concentration plus the triangle inequality to lower bound the same operator norm.

nodes.name: Combine the two bounds
nodes.statement: Finally, we combine two results and obtain \begin{equation*} |\Gamma|\cdot |\Omega| \geq \frac{\left\| \Vm_{\Omega} \Um_{\Omega} \Id_{\Gamma} \right\|_2^2}{\left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 } \ > \ \frac{ (1 - (\epsilon_{\Omega} + \epsilon_{\Gamma} ))^2 }{ \left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Chain the upper and lower bounds to get the uncertainty inequality.

nodes.name: The lower bound depends on the maximum magnitude of the graph Fourier basis
nodes.statement: We see that the lower bound involves with the maximum magnitude of $\Um_{\Omega}$. In classical signal processing, $\Um$ is the discrete Fourier transform matrix, so $\left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty} = 1/\sqrt{N}$; the lower bound is $O(N)$ and signals cannot localize in both time and frequency domain. However, for complex and irregular graphs, the energy of a graph Fourier basis vector may concentrate on a few elements, that is, $\left\| \Um_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty} = O(1)$, as shown in Figures~\ref{fig:geo_fourier}(a)(b)(c)(d). It is thus possible that graph signals can be localized in both the vertex and spectrum domain.
nodes.statement_short: Because $\|\Um_\Omega\|_\infty$ can be $O(1)$ on irregular graphs, unlike $1/\sqrt{N}$ for the DFT, joint vertex-spectrum localization becomes possible.

nodes.name: Localization of a graph signal
nodes.statement: The \textit{localization} of a graph signal means that most elements in a graph signal are zeros, or have small values; only a small number of elements have large magnitudes and the corresponding nodes are clustered in one subgraph with a small diameter.
differentia: most elements in a graph signal are zeros, or have small values
only a small number of elements have large magnitudes and the corresponding nodes are clustered in one subgraph with a small diameter

nodes.name: Inverse participation ratio (IPR)
nodes.statement: Prior work uses~\emph{inverse participation ratio} (IPR) to quantify localization~\cite{CucuringuM:11}. The IPR of a graph signal $\x \in \R^N$ is \begin{equation*} {\rm IPR} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^{4}}{(\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^{2})^2}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Shortcomings of the inverse participation ratio
nodes.statement: A large IPR indicates that $\x$ is localized, while a small IPR indicates that $\x$ is not localized. The range of IPR is from $0$ to $1$. For example, $\x=[1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N},\cdots,1/\sqrt{N}]^T$ is the most delocalized vector with $\text{IPR}=1/N$, while $\x=[1,0,\cdots,0]^T$ is the most localized vector with $\text{IPR}=1$. IPR has some shortcomings: a) IPR only promotes sparsity, that is, a high IPR does not necessarily mean that the nonzero elements concentrate in a clustered subgraph, which is the essence of localization (Figure ~\ref{fig:cluster}); b) IPR does not work well for large-scale datasets. When $N$ is large, even if only a small set of elements are non zero, IPR tends to be small.
nodes.statement_short: IPR only captures sparsity, not clustering, and degrades for large $N$.

nodes.name: Energy concentration ratio (ECR)
nodes.statement: We use \textit{energy concentration ratio} (ECR) to quantify the energy concentration property. The ECR is defined as \begin{equation*} \rm{ECR} = \frac{S^*}{N}, \end{equation*} where $S^*$ is the smallest $S$ that satisfies $ \left\| \x_S \right\|_2^2 \geq 95\% \left\| \x \right\|_2^2, $ with $\x_S$ the first $S$ elements with the largest magnitude in $\x$.
nodes.genus: measure to quantify the energy concentration property
differentia: $\rm{ECR} = \frac{S^*}{N}$
$S^*$ is the smallest $S$ that satisfies $\left\| \x_S \right\|_2^2 \geq 95\% \left\| \x \right\|_2^2$

nodes.name: Normalized geodesic distance (NGD)
nodes.statement: We next use \textit{normalized geodesic distance} (NGD) to quantify the clustered property. Let $\M$ be the set of nodes that possesses 95\% energy of the whole signal. The normalized geodesic distance is defined as: \begin{equation*} {\rm{NGD}} = \frac{1}{D}\frac{\sum_{ i, j \in \M, i \neq j}d(v_i,v_j)}{n(n-1)/2}, \end{equation*} where $D$ is the diameter of the graph, $d(v_i,v_j)$ is the geodesic distance between nodes $i$ and $j$.
nodes.genus: measure to quantify the clustered property
differentia: ${\rm{NGD}} = \frac{1}{D}\frac{\sum_{ i, j \in \M, i \neq j}d(v_i,v_j)}{n(n-1)/2}$
$\M$ is the set of nodes that possesses 95\% energy of the whole signal

nodes.name: Localized graph Fourier basis
nodes.statement: Each graph Fourier basis vector is regarded as a graph signal. When most basis vectors in the graph Fourier basis are localized, that is, the corresponding ECRs and NGDs are small, we call that graph Fourier basis localized.
differentia: most basis vectors in the graph Fourier basis are localized, that is, the corresponding ECRs and NGDs are small

nodes.name: arXiv GrQc collaboration network
nodes.statement: We now investigate the localization phenomenon of graph Fourier bases of several real-world networks, including the arXiv general relativity and quantum cosmology (GrQc) collaboration network~\cite{LeskovecKF:07}, arXiv High Energy Physics - Theory (Hep-Th) collaboration network~\cite{LeskovecKF:07} and the Facebook `friend circles' network~\cite{LeskovecKF:07}. We find similar localization phenomena among different datasets. Due to the limited space, we only show the result of arXiv GrQc collaboration network. The arXiv GrQc network represents the collaborations between authors based on the submitted papers in general relativity and quantum cosmology category of arXiv. When the author $i$ and author $j$ coauthored a paper, the graph contains an undirected edge between node $i$ and $j$. The graph contains 5242 nodes and 14496 undirected edges. Since the graph is not connected, we choose a connect component with 4158 nodes and 13422 edges.
nodes.statement_short: Localization is studied on the arXiv GrQc coauthorship graph (4158-node connected component).

nodes.name: Graph Fourier basis vectors of real networks are localized
nodes.statement: We find that a large number of graph Fourier basis vectors has small ECRs and NGDs, which indicates that graph Fourier basis vectors of various graph representation matrices are localized. Among various graph representation matrices, the graph Fourier basis vectors of graph Laplacian matrix tend to be more localized, especially in high-frequency components. In low-frequency components, the graph Fourier basis vectors of adjacency matrix are more localized.
nodes.statement_short: Empirically, graph Fourier basis vectors are localized; Laplacian bases localize in high frequencies, adjacency bases in low frequencies.
assumptions: a large number of graph Fourier basis vectors has small ECRs and NGDs
conclusions: graph Fourier basis vectors of various graph representation matrices are localized
the graph Fourier basis vectors of graph Laplacian matrix tend to be more localized, especially in high-frequency components
In low-frequency components, the graph Fourier basis vectors of adjacency matrix are more localized

nodes.name: New role of the graph Fourier transform
nodes.statement: The Fourier transform is famous for capturing the global behaviors and works as a counterpart of the delta functions; however, this may not be true on graphs. The study of new role of the graph Fourier transform will be an interesting future work.

nodes.name: Nonlinear approximation
nodes.statement: We consider nonlinear approximation for the graph Fourier bases, that is, after expanding with a representation, we should choose the $K$ largest-magnitude expansion coefficients so as to minimize the approximation error. Let $\{ \phi_k \in \R^N \}_{k=1}^N$ and $\{ \widehat{\phi}_k \in \R^N \}_{k=1}^N$ be a pair of biorthonormal basis and $\x \in \R^N $ be a signal. Here the graph Fourier transform matrix $\Um = \{ \widehat{\phi}_k \}_{k=1}^N$ and the graph Fourier basis $\Vm = \{ \phi_k \}_{k=1}^N$. The nonlinear approximation to $\x$ is \begin{eqnarray} \x^* = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_K} \left\langle {\x, \widehat{\phi}_k} \right\rangle \phi_k, \end{eqnarray} where $\mathcal{I}_K$ is the index set of the $K$ largest-magnitude expansion coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Expand a signal in a biorthonormal basis and keep the $K$ largest-magnitude coefficients.
input: a pair of biorthonormal basis $\{ \phi_k \in \R^N \}_{k=1}^N$ and $\{ \widehat{\phi}_k \in \R^N \}_{k=1}^N$
$\mathcal{I}_K$ is the index set of the $K$ largest-magnitude expansion coefficients

nodes.name: Expand in the representation and select the largest coefficients
nodes.statement: after expanding with a representation, we should choose the $K$ largest-magnitude expansion coefficients so as to minimize the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Select the index set of the $K$ largest-magnitude coefficients.

nodes.name: Reconstruct from the selected coefficients
nodes.statement: The nonlinear approximation to $\x$ is \begin{eqnarray} \x^* = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_K} \left\langle {\x, \widehat{\phi}_k} \right\rangle \phi_k, \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Return the partial reconstruction over the retained index set.

nodes.name: Sparse coding with the graph polynomial dictionary
nodes.statement: Since the the graph polynomial dictionary is redundant, we solve the following sparse coding problem, \begin{eqnarray} \x^* = & \arg \min_{\a} & \left\| \x - \D_{\rm poly(2)} \a \right\|_2^2, \\ \nonumber & {\rm subject~to:~} & \left\| \a \right\|_0 \leq K, \end{eqnarray} where $\D_{\rm poly(2)}$ is the graph polynomial dictionary with order $2$ and $\a$ are expansion coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: $\ell_2$ sparse coding of $\x$ over the order-2 graph polynomial dictionary with at most $K$ atoms.

nodes.name: Orthogonal matching pursuit
nodes.statement: We solve~\eqref{eq:sparse_coding} by using the orthogonal matching pursuit, which is a greedy algorithm~\cite{PatiRK:93}.
nodes.statement_short: Greedy atom selection to solve the sparse coding problem.

nodes.name: Normalized mean square error
nodes.statement: we evaluate the approximation error by using the normalized mean square error, that is, \begin{equation} {\rm Normalized~MSE} = \frac{ \left\| \x^* - \x \right\|_2^2 }{ \left\| \x \right\|_2^2 }, \end{equation} where $\x^*$ is the approximation signal and $\x$ is the original signal.

nodes.name: Wind speed on the Minnesota road graph
nodes.statement: The Minnesota road graph is a standard dataset including 2642 intersections and 3304 roads ~\cite{MinnesotaGraph}. we construct a graph by modeling the intersections as nodes and the roads as undirected edges. We collect a dataset recording the wind speeds at those 2642 intersections~\cite{JiCVK:15}. The data records the hourly measurement of the wind speed and direction at each intersection. In this paper, we present the data of wind speed on January 1st, 2015. Figure~\ref{fig:smooth_app_wind}(a) shows a snapshot of the wind speeds on the entire Minnesota road. The expansion coefficients obtained by using four representations are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:smooth_app_wind}(b), (c), (d) and (e). The energies of the frequency coefficients of $\Vm_{\W}$, $\Vm_{\LL}$ and $\Vm_{\Pj}$ mainly concentrate on the low-frequency bands; $\Vm_{\LL}$ and $\Vm_{\Pj}$ are more concentrated; $\D_{\rm poly(2)}$ is redundant and the corresponding expansion coefficients $\D_{\rm poly(2)}^T \x$ are not sparse.
nodes.statement_short: Approximation of Minnesota road-graph wind speeds under four representations.

nodes.name: Temperature on the U.S weather station graph
nodes.statement: The U.S weather station graph is a network representation of $150$ weather stations across the U.S. We assign an edge when two weather stations are within 500 miles. The graph includes $150$ nodes and $1033$ undirected, unweighted edges. Each weather station has $365$ days of recordings (one recording per day), for a total of 365 graph signals. As an example, see Figure~\ref{fig:smooth_app_temp}(a). The expansion coefficients obtained by using four representations are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:smooth_app_temp}(b), (c), (d) and (e). Similarly to the wind speed dataset, the energies of the frequency coefficients of $\Vm_{\W}$, $\Vm_{\LL}$ and $\Vm_{\Pj}$ are mainly concentrated on the low-frequency bands; $\Vm_{\LL}$ and $\Vm_{\Pj}$ are more concentrated; $\D_{\rm poly(2)}$ is redundant and the corresponding expansion coefficients $\D_{\rm poly(2)}^T \x$ are not sparse.
nodes.statement_short: Approximation of U.S. weather-station temperatures under four representations.

nodes.name: Preferred smoothness criteria and dictionary for real-world smooth graph signals
nodes.statement: The results from two real-world datasets suggest that we should consider using pairwise Lipschitz smooth, total Lipschitz smooth and local normalized neighboring smooth criteria to model real-world smooth graph signals. In terms of the representation dictionary, among $\Vm_{\LL}$, $\D_{\rm poly(2)}$ and $\Vm_{\Pj}$, $\D_{\rm poly(2)}$ is redundant; $\Vm_{\Pj}$ is not orthonormal. We thus prefer using $\Vm_{\LL}$ because it is an orthonormal basis.
nodes.statement_short: Experiments favour the pairwise/total Lipschitz and local normalized criteria, and $\Vm_\LL$ as the dictionary.
assumptions: The results from two real-world datasets
conclusions: we should consider using pairwise Lipschitz smooth, total Lipschitz smooth and local normalized neighboring smooth criteria to model real-world smooth graph signals
We thus prefer using $\Vm_{\LL}$ because it is an orthonormal basis
